# Laṭukikajātaka (Ja 357)
**ID:** Ja 357
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Laṭukikajātaka* (Ja 357), rendered in English as *The Quail*, is a canonical tale in the Pali Jātaka collection [SuttaCentral]. The narrative framework is set at the Bamboo Grove (Veḷuvana) in Rājagaha, where the Buddha overhears the monks discussing the cruel, harsh, and pitiless behavior of Devadatta [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1883]. The Buddha remarks that Devadatta was devoid of compassion in past lives as well, introducing a tale of the past that opens with the verse verse-line *Vandāmi taṁ kuñjara saṭṭhihāyanaṁ* ("Elephant of sixty years") [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1883]. In the past story, the Bodhisatta was born as a majestic leader of a herd of eighty thousand elephants in the Himālayas, while Devadatta was a solitary rogue elephant (*ekacārihatthī*) [Fausböll 1883; Cunningham 1879]. When a mother quail (*laṭukikā*) nests in the forest path, the Bodhisatta shields her fledglings, but the arrogant rogue elephant intentionally tramples the young birds to death [Fausböll 1883; Cunningham 1879; UNDV Conference Volume 2009].
Seeking vengeance, the small bird devises a plan with three allies—a crow that pecks out the elephant's eyes, a fly that infests the wounds, and a frog whose croaking lures the blinded elephant over a precipice to his death [Cunningham 1879]. Alexander Cunningham highlighted that this story is represented in 3rd-century BCE bas-relief sculptures at the Bharhut Stupa, closely matching the details preserved in the Pali tradition [Cunningham 1879]. The Jātaka commentary cites the defeat of the powerful elephant by the small quail as an exemplary demonstration of strategic wisdom (*ñāṇakusalatā*) overcoming mere physical brute strength [Fausböll 1891], while modern scholars note the story's moral warning against the arrogant abuse of power [UNDV Conference Volume 2009].
SuttaCentral registers four translations across four languages [SuttaCentral]. Text-reuse analysis via DharmaNexus identifies 9 matching segments (totaling 897 characters; longest §4.4–5.6 ↔ §1497–1499) with the third volume of the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus detects no cross-language alignments with Chinese, Sanskrit, or Tibetan collections meeting the threshold score of 10 [DharmaNexus].
